rationale: This anthropological study examines conceptual metaphors and cultural understandings of flowing water around a hydroelectric dam, mountain pastures, and sacred sites in Kyrgyzstan to critique social-science theories of 'flow'. It does not examine household or community domestic water or sanitation service access (E07), any legal/administrative/institutional mechanism governing service access, or any service access outcome.
plain_vs_narrow_note: Excluded under both narrow and plain Criterion 2 readings: the study focuses on cultural metaphors of landscape/hydroelectric/pastoral/sacred water rather than domestic water or sanitation service access or any legal, administrative, or governance mechanism.

evidence_quotes.quote: understand and interact with water in three highly significant places: mountain pastures (jailoos), the Toktogul hydroelectric dam that controls the flow of the Naryn and sacred sites (mazars).

Contrasting how metaphors of running water are put to use conceptually by Toktogul residents and social scientists opens up a critique of current academic and policy-oriented descriptions of the world as 'flow'.
